There are two important cues for locating a sound source: spatial cues and spectral cues.

Spatial cues

Good old Lord Rayleigh turns up again. His duplex theory, proposed in 1906, describes how we localize sound with two ears. The spatial cues are the interaural time difference (ITD) and the interaural level difference (ILD). The former works for low-frequency sounds, the latter for high frequencies.

At low frequencies (roughly 80 Hz < frequency < 800 Hz), sound diffracts around the head, so the levels at the left and right ears hardly differ. But we can tell the direction from the phase difference, that is, from the difference in the time the sound takes to reach each ear.

At high frequencies, the wavelength is so short that the ITD already amounts to several wavelengths, so it can no longer tell us the direction. This is where a big head comes in handy: when sound arrives from one side, the head blocks its path to the other ear, so the level difference is very clear.

Spatial cues, however, only really explain how we locate sources off to either side, or sources in the horizontal plane. The human ear is more capable than we might think.

Spectral cues

The head, the ears and the shoulders together act as a spatial filter on sound. I mentioned this in the answer below:

How does the ear tell high notes from low ones?

For example, close your eyes and have a high-frequency sound played first in front of you and then behind you. Because of the peculiar shape of the pinna, the sound reflects off it differently in each case, so the sound reaching the inner ear is different, and that is how we can tell whether it is in front or behind. This is called a spectral cue. Of course, it only works for high-frequency sounds. At low frequencies the wavelength is so long that, with our eyes closed, we find it hard to tell front from back.

Spectral cues help us partly resolve the cone of confusion at high frequencies.

Still, the quickest and most effective fix is… let’s shake it!

Change up all those cues, and suddenly the sound is so easy to place!
